classification.difficultyReason: Requires a general proof of injectivity, surjectivity and the inverse of a composition.

content.prompt:
Suppose $f:X\to Y$ and $g:Y\to Z$ are both bijections. Prove that $g\circ f$ is a bijection and that
$$(g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}.$$

answer.short:
$(g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}$.

Injectivity follows by applying the injectivity of $g$, then $f$. For each $z\in Z$, the input $f^{-1}(g^{-1}(z))$ maps to $z$, proving surjectivity and the inverse rule.
answer.worked:
Injectivity. Let $u,v\in X$ and suppose $(g\circ f)(u)=(g\circ f)(v)$. Then
$$\begin{align*}
g(f(u))&=g(f(v))\\
f(u)&=f(v)\\
u&=v.
\end{align*}$$
The second equality uses the injectivity of $g$, and the third uses the injectivity of $f$. Hence $g\circ f$ is injective.

Surjectivity. For any $z\in Z$, choose $x=f^{-1}(g^{-1}(z))\in X$. The inverses exist because $f$ and $g$ are bijections. Then
$$\begin{align*}
f(x)&=g^{-1}(z)\\
g(f(x))&=g(g^{-1}(z))\\
g(f(x))&=z.
\end{align*}$$
Hence $g\circ f$ is surjective and therefore bijective. Its unique input corresponding to $z$ is $f^{-1}(g^{-1}(z))$, so
$$(g\circ f)^{-1}=f^{-1}\circ g^{-1}.$$
